items.title: Mortgage rates whiplash is in full effect, with jumbo loans shedding 25 bps this week
items.description: The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that's been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks. At HousingWire 's Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago. Rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) dropped 7 bps to 7.30%, while rates for 30-year jumbo loans plummeted 25 bps to 7.62%. Rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics. Last week's application index from the Mortgage Bankers Association showed that total applications were down 5% on a weekly basis. MBA data released Tuesday found that affordability is about 8% weaker than a year ago , even though it improved slightly from September to October. “Higher mortgage rates weighed on application activity last week, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.35%. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, reflecting continued affordability challenges and softer homebuyer demand. The direction of mortgage rates in the coming weeks will be key to the housing market’s momentum heading into 2027,” MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement. Dan Ribler , vice president of capital markets and strategy at national reverse mortgage lender Longbridge Financial , said that the October jobs report should've sent rates higher . Nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 positions last month and the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1%, indicative of today's healthier labor market conditions in relation to 2025. Ribler noted that the jobless rate has been below 5% every month since September 2021, unemployment claims are lower than a year ago and the Federal Reserve 's "own description is the labor market is very strong." But strong employment trends have been overshadowed by stubborn inflation , which continues to run well above the central bank's 2% annualized target. "Inflation has been above 2% year over year 57 months in a row," Ribler remarked. "The Fed has, by the way, under this administration, reiterated the 2% hurdle and that they're going to be tough on inflation. They're certainly talking the hawk talk, saying we're going to keep inflation under 2%. "But man, I don't know about you, if my kid breaks curfew 57 nights in a row — and I say I'm going to punish you one of these times and I never do anything about it — at some point, he stops believing me, right?" Inflation is likely to prompt the Fed to raise rates next month. The CME Group 's FedWatch tool reveals that a 25-bps hike in December is all but certain, with 96% of interest rate traders saying that the federal funds rate will rise to a range of 4% to 4.25%. It was last at that level in September 2025. Silver linings are hard to identify Much of the housing and mortgage industry headlines in the past week have cast a shadow over any potential market improvements in 2027. Selma Hepp , chief economist at Cotality , said in a statement that existing home sales have fallen to their lowest level since August 2010. She also pointed to a Realtor.com analysis, which found that the typical repeat buyer will pay about $1,100 more per month if they choose to sell and move. "A meaningful housing recovery requires rates to come down and, importantly, stay down long enough to improve affordability and unlock turnover," Hepp said. "Until then, the adjustment is likely to come through weaker sales and softer home prices rather than widespread homeowner distress. "The number worth writing is the $1,100. That's the jump in monthly payment a typical repeat buyer takes on just to move house. It's the clearest explanation yet of why nobody is selling." New home sales have been equally grim, with September's seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000 sales representing a 5.3% decline from a year ago. Higher rates have also prompted homebuilders to remain cautious about creating more supply, with U.S. Census Bureau figures showing that single-family housing starts were down 3.2% year over year in September. Monthly gains in total starts were largely tied to the multifamily sector. "Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October, the largest year-over-year drop since 2023," Zillow senior economist Kenny Lee said in a statement. "Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane." The relative lack of sales has weighed on mortgage origination volumes, with ATTOM data for the third quarter of 2026 showing that the roughly 730,000 purchase loans closed during that period were the lowest figure for any third quarter in 14 years. Refinance activity was also bleak, with the roughly 561,000 refis in Q3 down 19% year over year. Refi lending was down from Q2 2026 in nearly 90% of the metro areas analyzed by ATTOM, with the largest declines in major metros like San Jose, San Francisco , Dallas, Austin and Louisville, Kentucky. items.title: BTR sector fears Treasury rules move the goal line on investor ban
items.description: Earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn't know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out. Monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury 's public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban . Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands. BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into new projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules. Last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals. Treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption. Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , said in an interview with HousingWire TBD . Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including: National Apartments Association (NAA) and National Multifamily Housing Council (NMHC) National Rental Home Council (NRHC) Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) Up for Growth Action Berkadia LGI Homes Landmark Properties Quinn Residences AHV Communities A coalition of 12 developers, including Greystar and Brookfield Residential These letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow. Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed. The 18-month certificate-of-occupancy deadline The chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether. That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project. Richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences , argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell. “To build and stabilize a new community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross said in an interview. The letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold. The letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects. “A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read. Additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners' ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry. “If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and new construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read. To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction. Quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold. items.title: FHFA raises conforming loan limit to $855,400 in 2027
items.description: The baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be authorized to buy loans up to that balance in the vast majority of U.S. counties. The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates . The annual adjustment was 3.25% last year and above 5% in each of the prior two years. Under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline. For 2027, that ceiling will be $1,283,100 for one-unit properties in markets where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline limit. Conforming caps first surpassed $1 million in these high-cost areas in 2022. Special statutory provisions apply in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the 2027 baseline loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100, while the ceiling will be $1,924,650. “Due to rising home values, the CLL will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents,” the FHFA said in a statement. How FHFA set the 2027 limit Each November, FHFA publishes new conforming loan limits for the coming year. Increases resumed in 2016, after home prices returned to pre-Great Recession levels, a condition required by HERA. The statute also prevents the ceiling from declining in years when home prices fall; the cap only moves higher when national prices increase year over year. This year’s adjustment is tied to FHFA’s third-quarter 2026 House Price Index (HPI), which tracks changes in average U.S. home values over the prior four quarters. Nominal, seasonally adjusted, expanded-data HPI showed house prices rose 2.72% on average between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026, essentially matching the 2.71% rise in the baseline conforming loan limit. The new limits expand the amount of mortgage debt that can qualify for conventional financing backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . Loans above FHFA’s limits are classified as jumbos, a segment still dominated by banks and portfolio lenders that set their own credit standards and capital requirements. Mortgage lenders once again anticipated FHFA’s announcement and raised their internal conforming loan limits ahead of the official release to compete for volume. But they were conservative. Rocket Mortgage was an early mover, lifting its conforming loan limit to $845,000 for single-family homes in 48 states in September. CrossCountry Mortgage adopted the same level. Pennymac set its internal limit at $850,000, while United Wholesale Mortgage increased its one-unit cap for conventional and Department of Veterans Affairs loans to $847,440. items.title: Maryland Life Sciences Players Urge Coordination To Spur Growth
items.description: Suburban Maryland’s life sciences corridor has some of the most important pieces of the research and development puzzle already built in: the National Institutes of Health , the Food and Drug Administration and a deep bench of research and talent from universities like Johns Hopkins University and the University of Maryland. But more coordination is needed to fully harness the power of those scientific assets for the region’s growth and economy, panelists at Bisnow ’s Mid-Atlantic Life Sciences and Biotech Summit said this month. “This is our time to come together and to put ourselves on the map, and we do that by producing the science, by supporting our startups and by encouraging innovation and commercialization right here in this region,” Ecphora Capital Managing Partner Deborah Hemingway said onstage at the Bethesda Marriott. Bisnow/Emily Wishingrad Montgomery County Economic Development Corp.'s Prayas Neupane, Universities at Shady Grove’s Anne Khademian, Ecphora Capital’s Deborah Hemingway, Association of University Research Parks’ Brian Darmody and Stein Sperling’s Andrew Schwartz There is inherently a pipeline that those in the industry call “bench-to-bedside,” whereby basic research produces insight that then leads to real-world uses like patient treatment and diagnostics. But panelists said creating infrastructure around those collaborative efforts, concepts like innovation districts or centers of excellence, can boost the region from an economic development standpoint. “It's a collective effort, and we need to be thinking strategically around how do we market ourselves as a region, and how do we attract the companies that would have never thought about being here in that sense,” said Prayas Neupane, Montgomery County Economic Development Corp.’s director of economic development. From a real estate perspective, the idea would be to build structural hubs that can collate players across the life sciences spectrum — from academic institutions to private companies to hospital systems. In addition to enabling various players to collaborate scientifically, they would also help attract more companies and investment and provide a branding advantage for the region. “So why couldn't we create a Purple Line innovation corridor north and south, so you can actually bring together from a marketing standpoint FDA and NIH and College Park and NOAA and all of these assets,” Association of University Research Parks Chief Strategy Officer Brian Darmody said. The long-awaited Purple Line, which connects New Carrollton to the east and downtown Bethesda to the west, is tentatively set to open late next year. Darmody noted that there are three Maryland medical schools. In addition to Hopkins and UMD, there is also the federal Uniformed Health Sciences University in Bethesda. “We have these assets that are just sub-optimized because we don't have enough awareness of them, and I think if we collectively pull them together, that will make this region much stronger,” he said. Bisnow/Emily Wishingrad ATCC’s Rupali Lach, CannonDesign’s Charu McDermott, Whiting-Turner’s Colin Regan, Merrick and Co.'s Patrick Conley, Athari BioSciences Inc.’s Susan Mitchell, Sapient Biotech’s Bibhash Mukhopadhyay and Scheer Partners’ Matthew Brady Some efforts to create these kinds of innovation hubs in the region are underway. A 14-acre life sciences district next to the North Bethesda Metro station is in the works, set to be anchored by the University of Maryland’s Institute for Health Computing. The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority selected Hines as the developer for the project last year. MCB Real Estate , which is building Viva White Oak, a $2.8B mixed-use development next to the FDA, envisions 3M SF of office space with a focus on the life science industries . Onstage, Darmody called the Viva White Oak effort “needed,” but he said the county still has to be working toward attracting companies to fill that planned development. “Somebody, a new intermediary, whether it's Montgomery County EDC or a new regional enterprise, has to provide the strategy and the facilities and the financing to get more of that in the private sector,” he said. Panelists said the field of quantum sciences could be an opportunity to create a specialized hub in the region, given its preexisting strength in the space. But it's easier said than done, panelists said, as these efforts require the necessary coordination, funding, political will and patience from public and private partners to see them through. “We need to do a better job of communicating and really talking, and then doing, doing the real work,” Athari BioSciences Inc. CEO and founder Susan Mitchell said. “It's hard work. It's hard. It's long, it's tedious, and it's costly, but if we want to be the center of excellence, because the mid-Atlantic region is ripe for it, we have the tools, we have the people, we just need to do it. Stop talking about it and do it.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Brian Darmody , Deborah Hemingway , Food and Drug Administration , National Institutes of Health , Patrick Conley , Prayas Neupane , Purple Line , Susan Mitchell

items.description: JLL Arranges $77M Loan for Refinancing of Ameswell Hotel in Mountain View, California by Amy Works November 24, 2026 November 24, 2026 4 MOUNTAIN VIEW, CALIF. — JLL has arranged a $77 million loan for the refinancing of The Ameswell Hotel in Mountain View, located in Santa Clara County. Bruce Ganong, Michael Leggett, Mike Huth, Shalin Patel and Jade Lewin of JLL Capital Markets secured the floating-rate loan through Brookfield on behalf of the borrower, Broadreach Capital Partners. Developed from the ground up and delivered in 2021, The Ameswell Hotel features 255 guestrooms and 24,000 square feet of indoor and outdoor meeting and event space, including an infinity ballroom. The five-story hotel offers three food-and-beverage concepts, including a signature California cuisine restaurant, a quick-and-casual café and an outdoor wine bar and pool venue. Guestrooms feature floor-to-ceiling windows, premium bedding and a curated art program. Onsite community amenities include a fitness center, heated outdoor pool, electric vehicle charging and pet-friendly accommodates. items.title: Home Price Growth Held Steady in September
items.description: Home Price Growth Held Steady in September By Anthony Smith Nov 24, 2026 What does the data show? The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Index showed national home price growth holding steady through September, with the U.S. National Index rising 2.1% year over year, unchanged from August and pausing a climb that began in the spring. The 10-City Composite posted a 3.5% annual gain, down slightly from 3.6% in the prior month, and the 20-City Composite rose 2.6%, in line with August. This month's release reflects sales closing from July through September, a period when mortgage rates edged higher, with Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate averaging 6.54% in July, near 6.7% in August, and 6.86% in September. Seasonality also shaped the monthly picture: the non-seasonally adjusted National Index fell 0.3% from August, while the seasonally adjusted index rose 0.2%, a sign that part of the monthly softness reflects the normal fall slowdown. The market's momentum has weakened since September closed . Contract activity softened over the same stretch with pending home sales down 4.7% from a year earlier in August before setting a series record low in September. How did trends vary by region? Regional divergence remains the defining feature of this cycle. Chicago led all metros for a sixth consecutive month with a 6.9% annual gain, followed by New York, up 5.8% annually, and Miami, up 4.6%, which climbed into the top three after a comparatively weak 2025. Seattle posted the weakest reading for a fourth straight month at -1.9%, with Denver down 1.0% and Dallas down 0.9%. The nearly 9-percentage-point gap separating Chicago and Seattle underscores how localized this housing cycle remains. What is ahead for housing? Despite the steady headline, home values continued to decline in real terms for a 16th consecutive month, as September's 3.7% inflation reading outpaced the 2.1% nominal price gain by roughly 1.6 percentage points, up from about 1.3 points in August. Looking ahead, the rate and demand backdrop has become more challenging since September closed. After four weeks of declines, the 30-year fixed rate jumped back to 7.28% as of Nov. 19, pushed higher by hotter-than-expected October inflation and expectations for a Fed rate hike in December. The median existing-home sales price rose just 0.4% from a year ago in October, while asking prices were down 2.2% and months' supply reached its highest level since 2015. If financing costs stay elevated into the winter, the plateau in price growth could give way to renewed softening, particularly in supply-heavy Southern and Western markets.

                  U.S. House Prices Rise 2.5 Percent Year over Year;
                        Up 0.7 percent Quarter over Quarter
Washington, D.C. – U.S. house prices rose 2.5 percent between the third quarter of 2025 and the
third quarter of 2026, according to the U.S. Federal Housing (FHFA) House Price Index (FHFA
HPI®). House prices for the third quarter of 2026 rose 0.7 percent compared to the second quarter
of 2026. FHFA’s seasonally adjusted monthly index for September remained unchanged from
August.

Significant Findings
   Nationally, the U.S. housing market has experienced positive annual appreciation each quarter
    since the start of 2012.
   House prices rose in 48 states between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026.
    The five states with the highest annual appreciation were 1) Alaska, 8.2 percent; 2)
    Connecticut, 5.4 percent; 3) Wisconsin, 5.3 percent; 4) Indiana, 5.3 percent; and 5) North
    Dakota, 5.2 percent. District of Columbia recorded a 4.2 percent price decline.
   House prices rose in 82 of the 100 largest metropolitan areas over the previous four quarters.
    The annual price increase was the greatest in Greensboro-High Point, NC, at 8.9 percent. The
    metropolitan area that experienced the most significant price decline was Washington, DC-MD
    at 4.9 percent.
   All nine census divisions had positive house price changes year-over-year. The Middle
    Atlantic division recorded the strongest appreciation, posting a 4.9 percent increase from the
    third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026. The Pacific division recorded a 0.5 percent
    price increase.
   Trends in the Top 100 Metropolitan Statistical Areas are available in our interactive dashboard:
    https://www.fhfa.gov/data/dashboard/fhfa-hpi-top-100-metro-area-rankings. The first tab
    displays rankings, and the second tab offers charts.

The FHFA HPI is a comprehensive collection of publicly available house price indexes that tracks
changes in single-family home values across the United States. The data extend back to the mid-
1970s and cover all 50 states and more than 400 American cities. Drawing on information from
over 100 million home sales and refinance transactions, the FHFA HPI provides detailed insights
into house price trends at the national, census division, state, metropolitan area, county, ZIP code,

The National Rental Home Council (“NRHC”) welcomes the opportunity to provide comments

The NRHC is a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit trade association that serves as the leading

professionally managed rental housing. The NRHC is dedicated to raising the standards for rental

items.description: Mortgage Rates Trickle Down to 2-Week Lows By: Matthew Graham 1 Hour, 25 Min ago Mortgage rates are primarily driven by day-to-day movement in the bond market. Bonds have been taking cues from turmoil in the stock market--especially among tech companies. With the NASDAQ on track to close at the 2nd lowest level since mid-April, it's no surprise to find bonds and rates are doing fairly well. Today's rate movement was fairly muted with the average top-tier 30yr fixed rate only dropping 0.02%. Still, that's the best level in exactly 2 weeks. You may be wondering: if bonds are taking cues from stocks and stocks are near their lowest levels since April, why are rates still so far above their levels from April? The stock/bond relationship is far from the only consideration for bonds. In fact, there are many times where stocks are moving higher in price even as rates are dropping. There are other times where one side of the market is flat while the other is on the move. Bonds care deeply about inflation, other economic data, and overall bond market issuance levels. All 3 have been pointing toward higher rates for most of the year, but those same 3 factors often help the stock market. See Rates from Lenders in Your Area The present phenomenon (stock prices and rates moving in the same direction) didn't really kick into high gear until mid-October when concerns over the pace of AI infrastructure growth began weighing not only on AI-focused stocks, but also on the broader economic outlook. items.title: U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October
items.description: U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October Published on November 24th, 2026 by Dian Zhang Nationwide, home prices inched up 0.14% month over month in October, the smallest increase in six months. Home prices increased in 30 of the 50 most populous U.S. metros, with Miami and Montgomery County, PA posting the fastest price growth. Home prices declined in 20 metros, with Seattle and Riverside seeing the steepest declines. U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months. Loading data… Home Prices Redfin Home Price Index Case-Shiller Index Month-over-month change in Redfin Home Price Index Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months. This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here . Home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin's records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October. However, a buyer's market doesn't necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they're still higher than they used to be. That's holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” s aid Chen Zhao , Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, w e don't think prices will fall very much.” There's also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they've seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao. Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao. Home Prices Are Rising Most in Miami Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October. The biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%). On a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%). Home Prices Are Falling Most in Seattle The biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%). Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined. This report is part of Redfin's monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center . items.title: Case-Shiller: Phoenix home-price growth inches higher in September
items.description: Case-Shiller: Phoenix home-price growth inches higher in September by John Yellig November 24, 2026 The overall pace of home-price growth across the United States continued to increase on an annual basis in September despite large market variations: Chicago led the nation for the sixth month in a row, while Seattle remained in last place. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index rose 2.1% year over year in September, the same increase posted in August. Month over month, the index slipped 0.3%. S&P Dow Jones noted that home values actually fell in real terms for the 16th month in a row, as September's 3.7% inflation erased the 2.1% gain in prices. "Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns," said Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August, marking the 16th consecutive month in which U.S. home prices declined in real terms." In Phoenix, home prices inched 0.4% higher year over year and were essentially flat month over month in September. "Chicago led all metros for the sixth consecutive month, posting a 6.9% annual gain, followed by New York at 5.8% and Miami at 4.6%. Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the fourth consecutive month at 1.9%, followed by Denver (-1.0%) and Dallas (-0.9%)," Kaufman said. " Miami's rise is particularly notable: After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025." items.title: Raleigh's housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds
items.description: For years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing. New research from The Pew Charitable Trusts shows what happened when Raleigh, N.C., followed that playbook. Following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found. The result was a building boom, particularly for the townhomes and apartments the city's earlier rules constrained. This uptick in homebuilding made renting more affordable in North Carolina’s capital city, especially for middle-income households and younger residents. The report highlights how adding new housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minn., and Austin, Texas. The same dynamic is playing out across the Sun Belt, where many of the nation’s fastest-growing metros also have some of the loosest zoning rules, and where rents and home prices have dropped more dramatically than anywhere else in the country. Raleigh’s post-COVID zoning reforms Raleigh didn't rely on a single fix to make building housing easier. Its reforms combined a rewrite of its form-based code, an end to parking minimums, denser building near transit and a housing bond to support affordable housing. “Of all of the drivers of housing costs – population growth, an influx of high-income earners, high land costs and high construction costs – we have the most agency and direct control over restrictive zoning regulations,” Patrick Young, Raleigh’s planning and development director, said in a statement. Allowing more missing middle housing Raleigh's 2021 zoning reform, which expanded the city’s already-established form-based code, opened the door to more "missing middle" housing. It did so by replacing units-per-acre caps with physical standards such as lot size, yards, and building height. The changes legalized duplexes, triplexes and quadplexes in more residential districts and expanded where townhomes can be built. Under the new form-based code, further refined in 2022, builders can now construct small apartment buildings and tiny houses with up to two dwelling units on compact infill lots. As a result, builders can now construct missing middle housing in more of Raleigh's neighborhoods, a shift that Pew links to better affordability for middle-income and younger residents. Reforming transit-oriented development and parking requirements Raleigh eliminated its citywide parking minimums in 2022. That allowed developers to fit more housing units on each property and, in some cases, spared them the expense of building costly parking structures, which can often make a project too costly to pursue. The city also spurred housing growth by allowing taller, denser buildings near major transit corridors. Transit Overlay District zones allowed for an extra story along Bus Rapid Transit corridors, extending half a mile along some local bus routes. Additionally, a density bonus allows developers to exceed height limits by up to 50% if at least 20% of the extra units are designated as affordable, below-market units. Approving housing bonds to incentivize affordable housing The City of Raleigh approved an $80 million housing bond in 2020 that is projected to create at least 700 affordable homes, fund homebuyer assistance and help homeowners with home repairs. About $14 million has already gone to four developments totaling more than 240 units, while another $24 million in gap financing will back over 470 additional units, more than 90% of which will be affordable to households earning 60% of area median income or less. How these reforms contributed to moderated rent growth Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh added 16,884 housing units, growing its housing stock by 7.7%, even as the city’s population grew by 5.8% over the same period. Raleigh's housing growth also outpaced the state (5.7%) and national (3.2%) rates during that period. Of the 16,884 units added, roughly 2,000, or 12%, were affordable to households earning 80% or less of area median income (AMI), with Raleigh's housing bond funds helping support their development. Density bonuses contributed about 200 of those affordable units, accounting for 10% of the total. Additionally, Raleigh’s code changes intentionally shifted a large share of production away from detached single-family homes toward townhomes, duplexes and tiny homes. Since 2021, the city has issued more than twice as many townhouse permits as in 2015 to 2020, and has permitted more than 200 duplex units and over 200 accessory dwelling units (ADUs). As a result, average monthly rents rose at only half the national pace and fell in real, inflation-adjusted terms. Pew’s analysis estimates inflation-adjusted rents declined 15% from 2022 to 2025, and, as of 2025, the income needed to afford the city’s median rent dropped from 79% of AMI to 65%. Raleigh's experience mirrors a wider trend among fast-growing Sun Belt markets, where less restrictive zoning and fewer barriers to housing development have supported greater housing production and helped moderate housing costs. The South accounted for more than half of all U.S. housing starts between 2021 and 2025, while Sun Belt markets continue to lead the nation in rent and home price declines. According to Yardi Matrix's October 2026 multifamily report , rents fell year over year in 12 major US markets. The Sun Belt accounted for ten of those, led by Austin, Houston, Nashville, Tampa and Phoenix. The for-sale market shows a similar pattern, with home prices dropping disproportionately in the Sun Belt while climbing in the Northeast and Midwest. Related More: Affordability Homebuilders

items.description: Declining Conditions for Multifamily Missing Middle November 24, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments Multifamily missing middle construction declined during the third quarter of 2026, and the market is down on a one-year basis. The missing middle construction sector includes development of medium-density housing, such as townhouses, duplexes and other small multifamily properties. The multifamily segment of the missing middle (apartments in 2- to 4-unit properties) has generally disappointed since the Great Recession. For the third quarter of 2026, there were 4,000 2- to 4-unit housing unit construction starts. This was down compared to the third quarter of 2025 (6,000). Over the last four quarters, there were 16,000 such starts, down from the prior four quarter period (19,000). items.title: U.S. Industrial Leasing Tied To Data Centers Surges To 50M SF
items.description: The rapid build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure has not only spurred unprecedented development in the data center real estate sector, but it is also increasingly supporting the industrial sector in markets across the U.S. Through the first nine months of this year, industrial tenants supporting data center development and operations signed 50M SF of deals, far surpassing the full-year totals for 2024 and 2025, according to a new report from Cushman & Wakefield . Courtesy of Cushman & Wakefield Cushman & Wakefield's report found data center-related industrial leasing is growing and making up a larger share of overall industrial demand. These tenants are bolstering the supply chains needed to build and run data centers. Cushman found three types of tenants leasing the most space: third-party logistics providers using distribution space for data center equipment, building suppliers using warehouses for data center construction materials, and manufacturers of data center equipment storing inventory in digital infrastructure hubs. These data center-related industrial tenants made up 14% of all industrial leasing last quarter and 11% through the first nine months of the year, Cushman found — up from less than 3% in 2022 and 2023 and roughly 5% in 2024 and 2025. This industrial demand surge is supporting the 36 gigawatts of data center capacity under construction in the U.S., in addition to the 47 GW of operational capacity, according to the report. It says the associated supply chain has exploded this year, with imports of AI-related equipment growing 62% from last year to $659B. “Data center development is creating a physical supply chain that extends well beyond the campus itself,” Jason Price , Cushman & Wakefield's head of Americas logistics and industrial research, said in a statement. “Servers, power and cooling equipment, construction materials and replacement parts all have to be manufactured, stored and distributed, and that is now showing up as a meaningful new source of industrial leasing.” The firm said this trend is especially prevalent in the established data center markets of Phoenix, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth and Columbus, Ohio. And it is occurring in emerging data center markets like Kansas City, Austin-San Antonio, West Texas and Reno, Nevada. An industrial market report from JLL last month found overall U.S. leasing was up 38.5% year-over-year in Q3 — the highest quarter in four years — and was driven by logistics facilities supporting data centers. This activity has been driven by some of the biggest names in the AI sector. Amazon Web Services in September launched a partnership with logistics company Kuehne+Nagel to use its network to support the construction of new facilities, plus maintenance and expansion projects. Cushman said this partnership, in addition to a data center-related expansion from DHL , has helped drive industry leasing activity from third-party logistics firms. Fluidstack, an AI firm partnering with Anthropic on its data center expansion, signed a lease in June for an industrial park spanning more than 1M SF in Glendale, Arizona. Nvidia in March announced a partnership with Corning, which makes connectivity equipment for data centers, to develop three manufacturing facilities in Texas and North Carolina. “This partnership is proof that AI is not just a technology story. It is a manufacturing story, and it is happening here in the United States,” Corning CEO Wendell Weeks said in a March release on the deal. items.title: Capital Is There, But Dutch Real Estate Needs Stability, Tax Relief And Power To Unlock It
items.description: A stable, dependable government with predictable policies, lower transfer tax and more solutions for grid congestion. That is what Dutch real estate is asking Sinterklaas for this year, according to speakers at Bisnow ’s Netherlands State of the Market event, held at KIT, formerly known as the Royal Tropical Institute, in Amsterdam. Bisnow/Mike Phillips APG's Robert-Jan Footse, Vesteda's Astrid Schlüter, Hines' Jan Hein Tiedema, CBRE IM's Jan-Willem Bastijn and ABS Real Estate Finance's Bert van den Hoek While some of these issues may be a bit trickier to overcome than others, speakers were adamant that addressing them would help bring capital back into the market. Money is there, and investors are keen to deploy it under the right conditions. “In January our outlook of the Dutch market was fairly positive, and that’s what we saw in the first and second quarter: a lot of traction in the residential market, mainly driven by Dutch institutional investors and family offices,” said Jan Hein Tiedema, head of the Netherlands at Hines , which manages $91B (€83B) in assets across approximately 30 countries. Commercial real estate investment volume reached €7B in the first half of 2026, up 36% on the same period last year, according to CBRE Netherlands. It is forecast to hit €15B for the full year, which would represent a 15% jump for the full year. However, the market shifted after summer, and not necessarily for the better. “With interest rates rising, I see many deals postponed, delayed and renegotiated,” Tiedema said. “We’re facing it ourselves on the selling side as well as on the buying side.” That same cautious approach is evident in capital allocation, with investors becoming increasingly selective about how and where they allocate money. Hines had been attempting to sell a residential asset in Amsterdam in September that was initially perceived as a “great deal, with plenty of appetite,” Tiedema said. However, the bids received were below expectations, leading Hines to pull the sale. With interest rates likely to rise before they fall in the eurozone, investors are relying on income returns to make money, and rents are rising in all sectors for good assets because of limited new supply. So the question arises: Where is capital still going in the Netherlands? Robert-Jan Foortse , head of European property investments at APG , one of the world’s largest pension investors, said the company had committed about €3B to its residential development partner platforms, including a tie-up with CBRE IM . “Of that €3B, we’ve allocated roughly €1.5B to actual projects. The NAV at the moment is only €500M, so we have some way to go,” Foortse said, adding that it was looking at forward funding and turnkey development. The Netherlands is grappling with an acute housing shortage, which is estimated to be at 384,000 homes, or 4.6% of the housing stock, according to the Ministry of Housing and Spatial Planning. As such, many domestic investors are investing in residential property. But just because there is a lack of supply doesn’t make it a good investment opportunity, Foortse said. APG has a mandate to invest capital in the Dutch residential market, particularly new development, but finds it difficult to identify the right product with the right risk-return profile. “Which is interesting, or rather a bit disappointing, because we have the capital and we would like to invest to build those houses, but we can’t make it work,” he said. For every new development APG backs, it rejects six to 10 of them. Tiedema echoed this sentiment, saying working in the Netherlands as an international investor requires “a thick skin.” Hines manages capital for the Netherlands, Germany and the Nordic countries, and all three compete for the same pool of capital. With these markets looking more attractive at the moment, Tiedema said the Dutch market is a difficult sell. However, the Netherlands only has “to make a few changes to be relatively more attractive” than the countries surrounding it, Foortse said, as the aforementioned countries face their own struggles. Among those changes needed in the Netherlands? Political stability. The Dutch cabinet nearly fell apart last week after the VVD clashed with D66 and CDA over a proposed reform of the Box 3 wealth tax system. VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz threatened to withdraw from the minority coalition, but after four days of crisis talks, Prime Minister Rob Jetten reached an agreement to keep the cabinet, highlighting the fragile state of the government. “Every time we meet with the ministry, we say, ‘Can we please have some stability and predictability,’ because that makes it so much easier for international investors to invest because it will just lower their return hurdle,” Foortse said. “Effectively changing the policy increases risk, and increasing risk raises your discount rates. It’s so simple, and if you maintain stability, return requirements go lower.” A major blocker for both international and domestic investors is Dutch transfer tax, which does not exist in most European countries of a similar size. For commercial properties, the transfer tax is 10.4%. Edge CEO Boudewijn Ruitenburg said a developer who buys an end-of-life building, renovates it and then sells it pays the tax twice. “It’s just ridiculous. Business cases do not work. That is something that the government needs to solve.” Ruitenburg said. At the end of the day, what international investors are looking for is very simple, said Jan-Willem Bastijn , head of EMEA transactions at CBRE Investment Management . And the fix is within reach. “They are looking for relative value. And where can I find the best value from a risk-return perspective? If you want to be relatively good, you need to offer growth,” Bastijn said. items.title: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul Signs New Private Listings Bill
items.description: New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent. Late last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listing Act . The language of the bill requires that real estate listings be marketed in "at least one other publication, platform or website that does not require payment" or for the consumer to work with the brokerage for access. This follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June. The New York State Association of Realtors® strongly supports the bill. This becomes the latest crackdown on private listings, where a real estate agent markets a property to a limited list of buyers before making it public. Fair housing advocates say private listings raise discrimination concerns. One study from Bright MLS found private listings take longer to sell and don't guarantee more money. The listing must be accessible to the general public, "without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise or select group of licenses." Also, there can't be restrictions on some or all of the details in the listing, according to the language of the bill. The bill doesn't require a seller or lister to hold open houses or public showings if it violates any state or federal laws related to health and safety. And sellers can opt out, by signing a form that explicitly warns them that the listing will have limited visibility and possible impact on the price they get. New York can punish violators with a fine of up to $5,000 and suspension or revocation of their real estate license. Earlier this year, the state saw its inventory of homes for sale fall to a 30-year low . Private listings debate Washington and Connecticut have passed similar laws this year. Each has generally similar language in their bills, which also allow for opt-outs. A study from Zillow found the sales price of private listings was 1.3% less than comparable sales on the multiple listing service, costing the seller an average of $4,230 per sale. ( Realtor.com® recently struck an agreement with Zillow to show preview listings from brokers who participate in Zillow’s preview program, in an effort to boost market transparency.) Compass Inc., the real estate brokerage giant which has defended its use of private listings, said its recently unveiled See It First listings strategy complies with the law. It launched that program in September, which gives early access to homes that will soon be listed on the public market. Users don't need to work with a Compass agent to use it. "New York’s new law preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes, including the ability to use a See It First strategy to test pricing and gauge demand," a Compass spokesperson said. "See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market." Loading... Compass CEO Robert Reffkin has defended the company's listings strategy. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images New York has long struggled with housing affordability. The Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card gave the Empire State an F, the lowest rating possible. Hochul has emphasized affordability concerns and made a deregulation push to make home construction easier. “My administration is focused on making New York more affordable and liveable for every New Yorker regardless of age or income, and housing is central to that goal,” Hochul said last week. Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

items.title: Research Triangle's Biomanufacturing Surge Is Luring More Companies
items.description: Ongoing investment in biomanufacturing across the Research Triangle is drawing more companies to the region and boosting the market’s research and development sector. Large pharmaceutical companies, including AbbVie and Novartis, have committed hundreds of millions of dollars in the past year to expand their manufacturing operations in the region. Those investments are also attracting smaller biomanufacturing firms to the area, panelists said at Bisnow ’s Research Triangle Life Sciences Summit in Raleigh this month. “The ecosystem has been buoyed up by the large groups that have come here, and it has become very ripe and fertile ground for the smaller, medium-sized companies coming behind it,” Jonathon Keener, a partner at Helix Ventures, said at the Brier Creek Country Club in Raleigh. “That's what we're most excited about because that diversifies our economy here.” Wikimedia/Abhiram Juvvadi In January, contract development and manufacturing organization Alcami paid $6.7M for a 37K SF biologics lab facility in Durham. In April, pharmaceutical supplier NewLife Medicals expanded into Efland with its $4.8M acquisition of a 28K SF flex warehouse. And Ypsomed, a midsized Swiss medical technology company, is building its first U.S. manufacturing facility with a $200M investment in Holly Springs, with plans to open by the end of 2027. Shifting trade policies and increased demand for U.S.-based production have prompted the life sciences industry to put more of its focus on manufacturing. Manufacturing has become “a national priority,” sparking new demand from life sciences companies for “facilities that can support process development, pilot production and commercial-scale manufacturing,” Tyler Grimshaw, principal of architecture and engineering firm EwingCole , told Bisnow ahead of the event . Raleigh-Durham’s life sciences market is showing signs of stabilization, according to a Cushman & Wakefield third-quarter report . Nearly 2.4M SF of new life sciences space has delivered since 2021. In the third quarter, vacancy in the market fell to 26.4% from 28% in the same quarter of 2025, reaching the lowest level in two years. This year, absorption turned positive again following occupancy losses in 2024. Pexels/Pavel Danilyuk The Research Triangle has seen a slew of large biomanufacturing real estate investments over the past year. Last month, diagnostic imaging company Bracco Imaging announced a $230M investment in a manufacturing facility in Sanford, just south of the Triangle. In April, AbbVie announced a $1.4B investment to build a 185-acre pharmaceutical manufacturing campus in Durham, with completion slated for the end of 2028. And in May, Novartis announced plans to add a new $220M facility , spanning 56K SF in Morrisville, part of a $23B U.S. manufacturing and R&D commitment . After a period of large-footprint commitments, smaller biomanufacturing companies are also coming to the Triangle. “There's been a slowdown in some of the larger users — and there's definitely been an uptick in the more medium- to small-range-size users,” said Carolyn Coia, vice president of real estate at Research Triangle Park . Part of that uptick is also due to the Research Triangle’s talent pool, flowing from North Carolina State University, Duke University and other universities in the area. “What North Carolina is great at is producing the future employees” for pharmaceutical companies, said Michael Morgan, managing director of tenant representation at JLL. Life sciences employment in the Research Triangle grew 21% from 2020 through 2025, reaching more than 58,000 workers across more than 650 companies, according to a 2026 Wake County Economic Development report . The region's employment concentration sits at 2.64 times the national average, outpacing national growth benchmarks, the report said. Panelists expect continued life sciences growth as regional talent keeps bringing in companies. “Once they come with their first initial investment, putting their toe in the pond, they realize what that talent can do for them, and they quickly double down,” Keener said. items.title: 3 ways apartment firms can manage AI risk
items.description: 3 ways apartment firms can manage AI risk Looking for system vulnerabilities in their systems and training employees can help companies protect themselves in an increasingly hostile environment, experts at OPTECH shared. Published Nov. 24, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google A picture of the Las Vegas skyline. OPTECH 2026 was held there. Getty Images LAS VEGAS — In the past, it might have taken people at student housing firm Preiss six months to tap into the company’s data and get the answers they needed to answer a question or address a problem. Now, artificial intelligence allows the firm to get answers in seconds, Whitney Kidd, senior vice president of innovation and technology at Raleigh, North Carolina-based Preiss, said on Nov. 17 at OPTECH 2026 in Las Vegas. “We could sit here and talk for days and days on all of the positive benefits we've seen in our industry,” Kidd said of the technology, adding that AI can also help the company respond at a scale that it couldn’t in the past. “We can't hire enough people to manage that [testing] consistently,” Kidd said. But AI’s speed also brings risks, allowing hackers to find vulnerabilities faster. “AI didn't change the tactics that the bad guys use,” Jeff Ewing, vice president of security operations and engineering at 5Q Partners, said at OPTECH. “It just gave them an industrialized machine. It's faster. It's a bigger volume.” Here are 3 ways apartment executives can try to manage AI risks and protect their systems: 1. Identify weak spots Multifamily firms and apartment properties don’t lack for systems that hackers can target, and it starts with their networks. “Are you sure that all your identities are protected?” Ewing said. “Can you lose one password, get in a breach and have someone you don't know access everything you have?” There is also potential for immediate financial loss. “From a money standpoint, can a single email or a phone call that comes in actually get money rerouted somewhere that you don't know about from an exposure standpoint?” Ewing said. On the property level, cameras and access control systems can also become targets. Ewing suggested it's important to keep property systems separate from the corporate network to limit access in a potential hack. “If a property system, a printer on a property or an access control system got compromised for whatever reason, is it physically separated from the corporate office so the bad guys can't access them? " Ewing said. If systems are breached, firms need to know immediately. “Is anybody going to say, ‘Oh my gosh, this is broken,’ or is it going to be six months from now when you realize you've lost something?” Ewing said. 2. Identify and prioritize vulnerabilities Apartment firms need tools to spot vulnerabilities and figure out what to patch first. Northland Chief Information Officer Michael DiBenedetto called the process “continuous threat exposure management.” “Are there signals externally that would tell you that this is an active problem to be considered, and not just a potential risk that you can maybe prioritize at a different level or scale?” DiBenedetto said at OPTECH. Once firms have identified the vulnerability, they need to focus on remediation steps, according to DiBenedetto. Because AI can find so many vulnerabilities, companies can’t patch everything at once. Instead, they need to identify the tasks critical to running a business and protect those things. “The key is to build that profile so that you can take a punch in the face and your business still runs,” Ewing said. “This comes down to an operations problem, not just an IT or a security problem.” 3. Train employees Preiss wants every employee to use AI, but in “a controlled and constrained environment,” according to Kidd. “The approach that we have been working on at Preiss is to have access and training at every level, because we don't want to bring a super-user into a beginner training,” Kidd said. “And we don't want to bring a beginner into a super-user training.” Northland is thinking about how to train employees to recognize when prospects or residents are interacting with AI, DiBenedetto said. “If a resident might get a response from an invoicing assistant or some sort of other communication that was maybe AI-generated, does our staff know?” he said. “Do they know where they maybe should step in versus where they should end up saying not step in?” Training also, of course, helps apartment firms protect themselves from cybersecurity risks that are accumulating worldwide. “You cannot govern technology people don't understand,” Kidd said. “They need to understand this technology so that you can appropriately govern it, and they understand the risk that's associated with the tools that they're using.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.title: Local governments sue HUD over mixed-immigration-status rule change
items.description: Local governments sue HUD over mixed-immigration-status rule change The lawsuit argues the rule is “callous, ill-conceived, and illegal” and that cities lack shelter capacity to handle the resulting homelessness. Published Nov. 24, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Chicago is among the local governments suing the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule change that would require recipients of federal housing aid to provide proof of eligibility for all household members. Getty Images First published on Dive Brief: A coalition of local governments and public housing authorities filed a lawsuit Monday to halt a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that would block households with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal housing assistance. The rule, scheduled to go into effect Dec. 14, is “callous, ill-conceived, and illegal,” and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, the lawsuit states. HUD’s rule change could displace at least 15,500 mixed-status families, according to the suit, placing additional burden on localities’ already-strained homeless shelter and support systems. Dive Insight: Households with mixed immigration statuses have for decades been able to receive federal housing assistance, prorated based on the number of household members who verify they are U.S. citizens or have eligible immigration status, according to plaintiffs. On Nov. 10, HUD announced all recipients of federal housing aid would be required to provide proof of eligibility for all household members. “The final rule includes any tenants currently living in ‘mixed status’ households that have exploited regulatory loopholes by enabling illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens to latch on to those with eligible status,” the agency stated. The coalition filed their lawsuit Monday in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts. Other lawsuits challenging the rule have also been filed by states and Los Angeles-area tenant organizations and housing advocacy groups. “HUD’s Final Rule is a radical departure from the law and decades of past practice and regulations,” San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu, representing the city in the Nov. 23 lawsuit, said in a news release. “Cities across the country are coming together to fight this callous and illegal change that is designed to push immigrant families into homelessness.” Along with San Francisco, plaintiffs include Boston; Chicago; the City and County of Los Angeles; King County, Washington; New York City; Providence, Rhode Island; San Diego; Santa Clara County, California; Seattle, and eight public housing authorities. items.title: National Home Value Growth Holds Steady, Yet Miami Outperforms
items.description: National growth in home values was flat month over month in September as mortgage rates accelerated and inflation continued running hot. The value of single-family homes as measured by repeat transactions increased 2.1% year over year, same as in August, according to data from the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index released on Tuesday. However, home values fell in real terms for the 16th consecutive month, as September's 3.7% inflation rate outpaced the home value gain by roughly 1.6 percentage points, up from about 1.3 points in August. "Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns," says Rebecca Kaufman , associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. Across the 20 cities tracked by the index, Chicago yet again led the U.S. with a 6.9% annual gain. New York City took second place with a year-over-year increase of 5.8%, but Miami emerged as the month's surprise, finishing third with a 4.6% gain. "Miami’s rise is particularly notable," points out Kaufman. "After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025." Loading... On the other side of the spectrum, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the fourth consecutive month at 1.9%, followed by Denver (-1.0%) and Dallas (-0.9%), reflecting a persistent regional divergence. September also revealed a widening gap between seasonal weakness and underlying price momentum. On a nonseasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.3% and 0.5% month over month, respectively, while both rose 0.2% after seasonal adjustment. "That contrast suggests that some of the apparent monthly weakness reflects the normal fall slowdown rather than a broad deterioration in home prices," adds Kaufman. The latest Case-Shiller release reflects sales closing from July through September, a period when mortgage rates moved higher, with Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate averaging 6.54% in July, near 6.7% in August, and 6.86% in September. Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith notes that the housing market's momentum has lost steam in recent months. Contract activity softened over the same stretch, with pending home sales down 4.7% from a year earlier in August before setting a series record low in September . "Looking ahead, the rate and demand backdrop has become more challenging since September closed," says Smith. After four weeks of declines, the 30-year fixed rate jumped back to 7.28% as of Nov. 19, pushed higher by hotter-than-expected October inflation and expectations for a Fed rate hike in December. Loading... The median existing-home sales price rose just 0.4% from a year ago in October, while asking prices were down 2.2% and months' supply reached its highest level since 2015. "If financing costs stay elevated into the winter, the plateau in price growth could give way to renewed softening, particularly in supply-heavy Southern and Western markets," notes Smith. The Case-Shiller Index reports on a two-month delay and reflects a three-month moving average of home sales prices. Homes usually go under contract a month or two before they close, so the September report primarily reflects purchase decisions made in late summer. Although the index's price data is delayed by several months, it is considered one of the best available measures of changing home values, because it is based on repeat transactions on the same properties. items.title: Orange County Department of Education Starts Work on $21M Environmental Education Development
items.description: Orange County Department of Education Starts Work on $21M Environmental Education Development The Orange County Department of Education has broken ground on Rancho Soñado Inside the Outdoors Education Center in Silverado, a $21-million, multi-building campus in eastern Orange County. C.W. Driver Companies is the general contractor for the project, which will restore a longtime environmental education campus largely destroyed by the 2020 Bond Fire. Located at 8755 Santiago Canyon Rd., the 110-acre property will feature 19,885 square feet of new facilities designed to provide hands-on environmental education for students from pre-kindergarten through high school. The development includes a 3,637-square-foot multipurpose environmental education building, a 4,382-square-foot covered outdoor instructional area, four 823-square-foot educational pavilions, a 133-seat amphitheater, an administrative building and an outdoor dining pavilion. Designed to enhance wildfire resiliency, the campus will incorporate noncombustible construction materials, interior and exterior sprinkler systems and improved emergency vehicle access. Other improvements include expanded vehicle and bus parking, accessible learning spaces and native, drought-tolerant landscaping. The development team also includes tBP/Architecture, project manager Schoolhaus Advisors Inc. and landscape architect Conceptual Design + Planning Company. Construction is slated for completion in December 2027. Image: tBP/Architecture Connect Inside The Story C.W. items.title: Plano’s Flaming Peking Duck Is a Gimmick—and It’s Also Very Good
items.description: Live Poll Peking duck offers one of the great rituals in the food world. The cooking process itself takes multiple days to ensure perfectly tender meat and ultra-crisp skin. Then the finished bird is sliced with expert efficiency into morsels just the right size to be rolled into a pancake. The duck will come with a table full of trimmings and sauces. But what if we set the duck on fire? That’s the question asked by Lulu Modern Chinese, a Plano restaurant that recently celebrated its first full year in business and just welcomed a new executive chef, Natalie Deprez. Lulu verges on clubstaurant, boldly decorated with a rainbow of colored lights, silvery reflective surfaces on the ceiling, and huge faces on the walls. A DJ spins at times (weeknights are quieter). A cocktail bar serves specialty drinks starting at $13 and building up to a Kung Fu Panda, served in a panda mug, that combines baijiu, soju, and sake. And then there’s the flaming Peking duck, which, the internet tells me, was pioneered by New York restaurant Hutong in 2021. A cook will roll a cart out to your table, with the duck propped up on a metal frame. A server will place all the extra goodies—thin crepes, sliced scallion whites and cucumbers, hoisin sauce, pineapple chunks for palate freshening—on your table. Then the cook will take a small tureen of Malibu 151 overproof rum, set it alight, and pour it over the duck’s head. It’s a good show, of course. What follows when the flames die out may be even better. The cook expertly breaks down the duck and slices all its meat into bite-sized morsels. A sliver of crispy skin runs along the edge of every piece. The butchery process takes a few minutes; if you took your camera out to film the flames, you may run out of patience, but where the fire is a visual spectacle, the carving is a display of pure skill. If the resulting duck wasn’t good, the fire would be a gimmick. The duck is excellent. Some bites had an especially smoky tinge—flames at work?—but other than that, this is a classic recipe done right. My party of three ate every last slice, loading up crepe after crepe. The only real feedback I’d have for Lulu is this: more scallions, please. The tray was otherwise bountiful and exemplary. If you need a side veggie with your duck, consider Chinese broccoli stir fried with eye-popping amounts of ginger and garlic. Sometimes a restaurant only needs one great dish to succeed. That could happen for Lulu: its duck would make a great holiday meal. (Indeed, Lulu will sell take-home duck feasts, all sides included, for Thanksgiving; the duck is set aflame before it’s packed up, so you can put your lighter down.) But there’s at least one other big winner here. Shrimp shumai dumplings are generously filled for the price, with excellent texture to both the filling and the wrapper. There’s a generous kick of ginger and a dainty nasturtium leaf on each dumpling. Shrimp shu mai at Lulu Modern Chinese. Brian Reinhart Other appetizers were less successful on my visit. Scallion pancakes had the right texture, but not nearly enough scallions. Most perplexing was a signature dish so deranged-sounding that we had to try it: fried spring rolls filled with ground beef and mozzarella cheese, then topped with a creamy aioli. “This could be one of those things that sounds crazy but is actually genius,” I told my guests. It is not one of those things. But that’s fine. After all, flaming Peking duck most definitely is. A non-flaming version is available too, by the way, if you’d rather just eat good food without added fuss. I enjoyed the fire. Either way, it’s a showstopper.
