items.title: William A. Brewer III: The Audacity of Texas
items.description: Live Poll Home is where the heart is. Mine is in Texas. From the vast, sunbaked plains of West Texas, where the horizon meets a sky awash with amber, to the glittering Dallas skyline, to the Gulf coast beaches of South Padre Island, Texas is a land of extraordinary contrasts -- and needs no introduction. Once an independent republic, Texas has been a rugged frontier, a battleground for independence, a kingdom of cattle and cotton, an empire built on oil, home to tens of millions of immigrants, and an economic powerhouse whose reputation exports far beyond its borders. It is a state where fortunes have been reaped, sowed, and made anew. Where generations of pioneers, entrepreneurs, and dreamers have wagered everything on the belief that tomorrow can be better than today. The promise of the American Dream. But to me, the measure of Texas has never been the size of its territory, the wealth beneath its soil, or the height of its skylines -- it's the spirit of its people. The name "Texas" traces back to the Caddo word tejas, meaning "friends" or "allies." Its nickname, "The Friendly State," is a fitting inheritance for a place where strangers seldom remain strangers, where a handshake can seal a million-dollar deal, and where southern hospitality comes wrapped in a drawl and a smile a thousand miles wide. I've encountered ambition in every corner of this country. New York has it in abundance -- but in Texas, ambition is accompanied by an intoxicating optimism. I was born on Long Island, far from Tex Mex and bluebonnets. But, when I arrived in the Lone Star State more than four decades ago, I found a land where people believed that the scale of their ambitions are dwarfed by the possibilities at their fingertips. After all, if everything is bigger in Texas -- why shouldn't dreams be? Dallas was a city brimming with ambition when I arrived in the 1980s. Oil fortunes fueled towering office buildings, banks financed sprawling developments, and a new wave of entrepreneurs were already reshaping the city's commercial landscape. There was money to be made, certainly, but more importantly, there was a rhythm to the city that even the oil bust and economic turmoil of the late 1980s couldn't diffuse. Between the larger-than-life personalities and the ever-present entrepreneurial spirit, I wanted to be part of it -- and found my home along the way. In 1984, I co-founded what is now Brewer, Attorneys & Counselors with the conviction that a law firm could be every bit as bold and unapologetic as the city around it. Dallas was, and is, a place where the greatest currency isn't oil, wealth, or land, but the audacity of its people to imagine something greater -- and make it happen. That outlook suited me, shaped our business philosophy, and animated every bit of our decision making. Over the decades, I've had a front row seat as Texas -- Dallas in particular -- continued to supersede the grandest expectations of those who helped build it. But the transformation seen across the Lone Star State has hardly been confined to its borders and balance sheets. When I first arrived, Democrats dominated its politics. Then, the pendulum swung and Republicans captured statewide offices, presiding over decades of incredible economic growth. And just recently, the pendulum has swung once more. For the first time in over three decades, Texans elected Democrats to statewide office. James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and state legislator, will become the first Democrat elected to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since 1988. Gina Hinojosa defeated a three-term incumbent to become Texas' first Latina governor. Both candidates rode that quintessential optimism all the way to the ballot box with an unwavering belief in the possibilities. They exuded a determination to challenge entrenched powers and billionaires, as they put their faith in the uncorrupted optimism of the people whom they hoped to represent. I've traveled far and wide, but nowhere have I encountered that spirit quite as fiercely or abundantly as in Texas. Nestled between a barber shop and a pizza joint on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard in South Dallas, in the '90's, we opened a "storefront" as our pro bono office. Miles from the gleaming glass panes and bustling boardrooms of downtown Dallas, the Brewer Storefront was born of the same optimism. Why shouldn't the people of south Dallas have access to the same caliber of legal representation as the corporations whose names litter billboards and skyscrapers? Why should the circumstances of one's life determine the justice they could afford? So we made room -- and keep the lights on and the door open to this day. The same conviction gave rise to the Future Leaders Program, an undertaking we funded year after year, and the most rewarding investment of my life. The premise is simple: a child's future should never be constricted by their ZIP code. So, we brought together Dallas' finest educators from Dallas ISD and its private schools -- St. Mark's, Hockaday, Greenhill, and ESD -- to create something extraordinary. On Saturdays, classrooms that might otherwise sit vacant in North Dallas come alive with students from South Dallas. From 7th through 12th grade, these students eager to learn, to lead, and discover a world of possibilities beyond their front yard -- to discover what outcomes they can achieve with effort. As I watch these young lives unfold, I never worry what they will make of the Texas they inherit. I am confident that the businesses they will build, the conventions they will challenge, and the changes they will make will be the hallmark of an even better future for our state. If the past four decades have taught me anything, it is that the Lone Star State has a remarkable habit of exceeding its own expectations -- and I know our best yet to come. items.title: FHFA maps out FICO 10T rollout with broad eligibility by late 2028
items.description: The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for use by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . It also released an implementation road map that would make FICO 10T broadly eligible and retire Classic FICO by September 2028. The staged rollout, announced Tuesday, mirrors the VantageScore 4.0 timeline and is meant to give lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers time to analyze historic FICO 10T data, rework pricing and risk models, and update technology before a full transition, according to the agency. "The timeline below prepares lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers for the final step in credit score modernization: lender choice between FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0," the agency said. At the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T are expected to go live alongside the existing Classic FICO in January. Bob Broeksmit , president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued a statement of support following the announcement. “We welcome this milestone as it moves us closer to the industry's and FHFA’s goal of transitioning to true competition with two modernized credit score models," Broeksmit said. "We appreciate FHFA's desire to provide a clear and transparent roadmap for this process. Given the industry’s experience with the just-completed adoption of VantageScore 4.0, MBA will work with FHFA and industry stakeholders to expedite the implementation timeline responsibly. "MBA and its members will continue to engage with FHFA to establish meaningful competition for both credit scoring and credit reporting. Continued reforms to end the tri-merge requirement will further improve our credit reporting system and lower costs for borrowers. Today’s announcement is a critical next step." Staged rollout The FHFA initially validated both FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 for use at the government-sponsored (GSEs) enterprises in October 2022. In July 2026, Fannie and Freddie released historical performance data for FICO 10T along with additional VantageScore 4.0 data, a key prerequisite for lenders and investors to back-test new score models and recalibrate credit policy. A FICO 10T pilot is expected to begin around December 2027. In this “launch and refine” phase, lenders will deliver a subset of loans underwritten with FICO 10T while FHFA, the GSEs and industry stakeholders monitor data quality, pricing and delivery performance. Based on pilot results, FHFA expects upfront pricing grids and private mortgage insurer eligibility requirements, or PMIERs, to be updated to reflect the new score model. That step will be critical for secondary market execution and risk transfer structures that currently rely on Classic FICO. A limited FICO 10T rollout is targeted for April 2028, followed by a scale-up and transition phase that leads to broad eligibility around September 2028. During this final stage, FHFA plans to confirm industry readiness, fully implement Uniform Loan Delivery Dataset (ULDD) Phase 5, expand FICO 10T use across GSE channels and retire Classic FICO. FHFA emphasized that dates after November 2026 are targets and are subject to change. Pricing dynamics In October, Fair Isaac Corp. said it will hold its wholesale mortgage price at $10 for a bundle of its credit scores for lenders and brokers enrolled in its Preferred Program. The $10 price is available through participating tri-merge credit report resellers to lenders that commit to FICO under the program. It covers both Classic FICO, which has been the mortgage standard for nearly three decades, and FICO Score 10T, the company’s trended-data model. FICO is also preparing a new subscription-based pricing model for mortgage credit scores in 2027, sources told HousingWire . VantageScore 4.0, by comparison, has been offered at 99 cents per score , or at no additional charge when purchased alongside a FICO score through Equifax , Experian and TransUnion , which jointly own VantageScore. Bank of America Global Research , using data from Recursion , found that more than 170 lenders now pull VantageScore 4.0. Despite that breadth of use, only a small share of conventional loans are actually priced with VantageScore 4.0. In October, 20% of issuance reported a VantageScore 4.0, yet only about 8% of total issuance used the score model for pricing, according to the research. items.title: Lower mortgage rates could bring buyers back. What market will they return to?
items.description: The possibility of mortgage rates falling below 7% before the holidays is back on the table . In Tuesday morning's Analyst Insights update in HousingWire Intelligence , HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami noted that the 10-year Treasury yield had reached 4.89%, approaching the 4.85% threshold he is watching, though mortgage spreads still need to improve. But for housing professionals hoping to reengage buyers who stepped away from the market, mortgage rates are only part of the equation. The homes available, the prices sellers are asking and the competition buyers face may look considerably different from when those buyers last searched. Nationally, active single-family inventory stands at 894,692 homes, approximately 8% higher than a year ago. New pending listings increased 5.7% in the week ending Nov. 20, while new listings increased 1.2%. That increase in contract activity is encouraging, but the broader picture remains more complicated. HousingWire Data shows that 44 of 57 large metro areas (77.2%) recorded an improving ratio of new pending listings to new listings over consecutive four-week periods, even as pending activity remained below year-ago levels. During the comparable period in 2025, just three of 54 qualifying metros (5.6%) showed that same combination. An improving relationship between incoming listings and new contracts does not necessarily indicate strengthening buyer demand. And if lower mortgage rates do bring buyers back, the opportunities they encounter will vary considerably by market. Similar contract activity, different buying conditions Consider Denver and Kansas City, two metro areas averaging nearly identical numbers of new pending listings per week but offering buyers different inventory and pricing environments. Over the four weeks ending Nov. 20, Denver averaged 497 new pending listings per week, while Kansas City averaged 491. Both markets are experiencing substantially weaker contract activity than a year ago. That's where the similarities begin to fade. Denver, Colorado Active inventory is up 10.1% year over year. New pending listings are down 20.4% year over year. The median active list price is down 4.3% year over year, to $646,000. 54.3% of active listings have had a price reduction. Denver's housing market offers buyers a different landscape heading into the holidays, with more available inventory, lower asking prices than during the spring and widespread price reductions. For buyers who paused their home searches earlier this year because of affordability, Denver's changing inventory and pricing conditions provide a reason to revisit their options, even before mortgage rates move meaningfully lower. Kansas City, Missouri-Kansas Active inventory is up 25.6% year over year. New pending listings are down 17.1% year over year. The median active list price is up 5.9% year over year, to $393,000. 41.5% of active listings have had a price reduction. Kansas City's median asking price has declined from its summer peak as price reductions have become more prevalent, although median asking prices remain above year-ago levels. Kansas City offers buyers considerably more selection than a year ago. And while asking prices have moderated since the summer, higher median asking prices compared with last year could offset some of the affordability gains from lower borrowing costs. What these differences mean for returning buyers Both markets offer more available homes than a year ago, but the pricing environments are different. In Denver, a decline in mortgage rates could coincide with lower asking prices and more available homes. In Kansas City, greater selection and recent pricing adjustments may create opportunities, even though the median asking price remains higher than it was a year ago. Changes in median asking prices can reflect shifts in the composition of available inventory, not just changes in individual home prices. That's why examining inventory, asking prices and price reductions together provides a more useful assessment of local buying conditions than any one metric alone. Where contract activity is beginning to shift Another consideration is whether contract activity is already beginning to strengthen, even with mortgage rates above 7%. In Denver, weekly new pending listings increased across the four most recent reporting weeks: Oct. 30: 474 Nov. 6: 488 Nov. 13: 508 Nov. 20: 517 Cincinnati, Ohio, recorded a similar pattern, with weekly new pending listings increasing from 397 to 459 over the same period. But Cincinnati presents a different inventory and pricing environment. Its median active list price is up 1.9% year over year, and the market has 2.44 months of inventory, compared with 3.01 in Denver. While both markets have recorded three consecutive weekly increases in contract activity, buyers returning to Cincinnati could encounter a tighter inventory environment than those returning to Denver. Neither market has recovered to last year's level of contract activity, and several weeks of increases are not enough to establish a sustained recovery, particularly heading into the holidays. Still, these are developments worth monitoring. If contract activity continues to strengthen while new listings decline seasonally, competition for available homes could increase. items.title: Brookfield Slashes Value Of Investment In Retailers In Half
items.description: Brookfield has written down by 50% the value of its investment in a group of famous American retailers, including JCPenney and Aéropostale, Bisnow can reveal. Wikimedia Commons/Azt3r1x Third-quarter accounts for a property holding subsidiary of Brookfield Corp. showed that the value of the company’s investment in Catalyst Brands was written down from $551M to $276M in the period. The write-down gives a rare glimpse into the financial performance of a bold move by retail real estate owners Brookfield and Simon Property to invest in the brands that occupied big swaths of their malls. The investment was in part an effort to avoid large voids in their assets if the retailers went bust, particularly during the height of the pandemic. Brookfield teamed up with Simon in 2020 to buy department store chain JCPenney for $800M, with the beleaguered chain’s lenders retaining its property portfolio. The deal involved the JV paying $300M and assuming $500M of debt. In 2025, the duo merged JCPenney with Sparc Group, a retail company that owned the brands Aéropostale, Brooks Brothers , Nautica, Eddie Bauer and Lucky Brand, to create a new company called Catalyst Brands. The company had 1,800 store locations, 60,000 staff, $9B in revenue and $1B in liquidity, according to a press release at the time of the merger, but in February 2026, Eddie Bauer filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, and all 200 of its stores closed. Simon owns a 39% share in Catalyst, according to its third-quarter accounts, with the rest of the company owned by a combination of Brookfield, retail specialist Authentic Brands Group and Chinese e-tailer Shein . None of those companies disclose their ownership level. Brookfield declined to comment on the write-down in its investment or its ownership proportion. items.title: Why 16 MLSs want a united front against Compass in the battle over private listings
items.description: Compass International Holdings may have filed 16 separate antitrust lawsuits against 16 separate MLS, but according to court documents filed earlier this week, those MLSs are seeking to combine these lawsuits into one. In a motion filed on Monday to stay the lawsuit Compass filed against it, California Regional MLS (CRMLS) told the court that it and the other MLSs Compass has filed lawsuits against have asked to consolidate or coordinate the pretrial proceedings for the various Compass v. MLS lawsuits currently pending across the country in federal court in the Southern District of New York (SDNY). If the panel declines to select New York, the motion identifies the Western District of North Carolina and the Middle District of Florida as alternative venues for the consolidated litigation. According to the motion, the MLSs have also asked to include the two declaratory judgement lawsuits nine MLSs have already filed against Compass in the SDNY. "Compass has chosen to wage the same legal fight in courts across the country, creating unnecessary costs and the risk of conflicting rulings, ” Richard Haggerty, the CEO of OneKey MLS , said in a statement. "Each of the 16MLS organizations are challenging that approach. We believe these cases belong before one judge, and we will continue defending the cooperation rules that ensure no brokerage gains an unfair advantage by withholding publicly marketed homes from the shared marketplace." This request comes after Compass informed the SDNY court that it plans to file a motion to dismiss the declaratory judgement lawsuits or to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS. After months of posturing and clashes over policies, the legal dispute between Compass and the MLSs kicked off in earnest this September when Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings. Later that month, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin told a room full of MLS executives gathered at the Council of MLSs (CMLS) that he would sue any MLS that refused to give in to Compass’s demands. Legal back and forth Despite Reffkin’s threats, it was actually CRMLS that made the first move, filing a lawsuit in early October seeking a declaratory judgment that its policies on listing cooperation are “fair, procompetitive, and legally sound,” according to a company announcement. CRMLS has since been joined by New York’s OneKey MLS in this lawsuit, while MLSListings , Arizona Regional MLS , bridgeMLS , Canopy MLS , REcolorado , Hive MLS, and Doorify MLS have filed their own lawsuit , also in the SDNY, seeking the same judgements as CRMLS and OneKey. In the midst of these lawsuits hitting the court docket, Compass filed its own lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging that its rule unlawfully restrict how homeowners and their agents can publicly market properties outside the MLS. Roughly a month later, Compass reiterated those same claims in 15 separate lawsuits filed against 15 MLSs . MLS defendants in those lawsuits include bridgeMLS, Bay East MLS, Contra Costa MLS, MLSListings, The MLS-CLAW, San Diego MLS, Canopy MLS, Hive MLS, Doorify MLS, Arizona Regional MLS, Recolorado, NorthstarMLS, Houston Association of Realtors, Stellar MLS and OneKey MLS. In an emailed statement a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the filing is “a procedural request that does not change the substance of [Compass’s] claims.” “Each MLS applies its own rules, and the impact of those rules on agents, home sellers, and buyers is specific to its local jurisdiction,” the spokesperson added. It remains to be seen if court will allow the MLSs to consolidate their lawsuits. This is not the first time real estate industry defendants have sought to consolidate similar lawsuits. Several real estate brokerage defendants in the copycat commission lawsuits attempted to consolidate their cases, but their request was rejected. items.title: Home prices rose 2.1% in September, inflation rose faster
items.description: Inflation continued to outpace home price growth in September, according to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index released on Tuesday. The data for September shows that home prices rose 2.1% year-over-year, unchanged from a month prior , resulting in an index reading of 308.06. In contrast, inflation came in at 3.7% in September. “Nominal home prices remain resilient, but inflation is once again widening the gap between nominal and real housing returns,” Rebecca Kaufman, the associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices, said in a statement. “Consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August, marking the 16th consecutive month in which U.S. home prices declined in real terms.” Month-over-month the national home price index was down 0.3%. Arish [10:23 AM] HousingWire Data , which is more current than Case Shiller shows that home price appreciation cooled for the week ending on Nov. 20, 2026. According to the data, the median list price for a single family home was $425,000, down 1.2% from a month prior and 0.7% from a year ago. Metro level changes Case Shiller’s 10-City Composite index rose 3.5% annually to 330.38, down from a 3.6% annual increase in August. The 20-City index posted a 2.6% annual increase, the same as a month prior, coming in at a reading of 318.73. Both the 10-City and 20-City index recorded a 0.5% month-over-month decline prior to seasonal adjustment. Of the 20 cities analyzed, Chicago was yet again the strongest market for home price growth, posting a 6.9% annual increase, followed by New York (5.8%) and Miami (4.6%). “Miami’s rise is particularly notable: After moving into fourth place among the 20 cities in July and August, it has now climbed into the top three, a sharp reversal from its comparatively weak performance in 2025,” Kaufman said. This is the fourth consecutive month Seattle recorded the largest annual home price decline. Santa Barbara, however, reported the largest annual price decline at -30.2%, followed by Fond du Lac, Wisconsin (-24.3%) and Dubuque, Iowa (-20.7%). items.title: ICE Buys 2 Detention Centers At Nearly 7 Times Appraised Value
items.description: The federal government acquired two detention centers from the private prison industry’s top publicly traded firms at prices that are more than six times their combined valuations, separate investigations uncovered. Unsplash/Larry Farr U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement paid Geo Group $453M for the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, after the detention center operator disclosed its book value was $67M, The Intercept reported . The federal government also paid $496M to CoreCivic for a facility in Appleton, Minnesota, that the other large publicly traded operator in the space had offered to sell to the state in 2025 for $75M, records separately obtained by NBC affiliate KARE 11 found . The $949M in sales volume for two properties with a combined appraised value of $142M has drawn questions from advocacy organizations and at least one senator in the weeks after Democrats swept both houses of Congress , setting the stage for investigations into President Donald Trump ’s strategies on immigration and other policies. “This new report is worthy of serious investigation and is part of a pattern of Department of Homeland Security purchases of detention facilities for hundreds of millions of dollars more than they seem to be worth,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, a Democrat from New Hampshire and the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, told The Intercept in a statement. “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.” CoreCivic said in a statement to Bisnow that the reported $75M appraisal figure was a preliminary number dating back to 2015 and not an accurate assessment of the property's real value. "The federal purchase price reflects what it would cost to build a facility of equivalent square footage and security at today’s construction prices, less depreciation," a spokesperson said in a statement. Geo Group declined to comment. The $67M valuation for the Geo Group property came from a document reporting its depreciated book value as opposed to an appraised book value. A DHS spokesperson said the acquisition of the two facilities strengthened the country's ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations. “ICE is regularly audited and inspected by external agencies to ensure that all ICE facilities comply with performance-based national detention standards," according to the statement, which didn't directly address the purchase price of the properties. CoreCivic sold four detention facilities to the government for a combined $2.2B in the third quarter, the company disclosed on Nov. 4. Among them is the 34-year-old prison in Appleton, with a population of less than 1,400, that has been closed for 16 years but was sold to the federal government for a nine-figure price. The $496M sale price was more than six times the price at which CoreCivic offered to sell the property to the state of Minnesota just a year earlier, records obtained by KARE 11 indicate. Minnesota Corrections Commissioner Paul Schnell called the price unexplainable and told the outlet he was stunned by the deal. CoreCivic has been using funds from property sales to pay down debt and repurchase stock. In the third quarter, it authorized a $500M accelerated repurchase plan. Shares in the firm are up more than 50% this year. Geo Group, which has seen its valuation rise more than 80% this year, said in third-quarter disclosures that it had made a deal on Nov. 17 to sell the 1,635-bed facility in Tacoma to the federal government. The deal was expected to generate roughly $340M in net proceeds that would help fund its own $500M accelerated share repurchase program. Geo Group submitted a $67M valuation for the property to the federal government in March 2026 as part of reporting requirements for a federal contract, The Intercept reported. As part of the sales, the federal government also signed contracts with Geo Group and CoreCivic to operate the facilities, according to disclosures from both companies. The two private detention center operators have seen their valuations soar in recent years. The reelection of Trump on a tough anti-immigration platform provided the first boost , but the firms have also benefited from the administration's shift away from plans to convert warehouses into detention facilities. Geo Group sold three other facilities to the federal government in October for a combined $950M. ICE paid $1.5B to acquire two CoreCivic properties in July. Cushman & Wakefield has been brought in to sell the warehouses the federal government acquired when it was initially planning to convert the properties into detention centers. items.title: What will Social Security look like in 2027 and beyond?
items.description: With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, quickly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels. Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration ’s recently announced 3.6% COLA for 2027. But Morningstar noted this week that the 2027 COLA — the largest since 2023's 8.7% adjustment — will translate into smaller take-home increases once Medicare costs are deducted. Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks. Morningstar reported that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 next year to $209.40, a 3.2% increase. That will allow most beneficiaries to keep more than 3% of the 3.6% COLA after the deduction. Morningstar calculated that a retiree receiving the average October benefit of $2,092 would see a net benefit increase of about 3.29%, assuming they pay the standard Part B premium and have no other changes in deductions. A higher-income retiree with a $3,500 monthly benefit would see a net increase of roughly 3.41% under the same assumptions. The COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which compares the average readings for July, August and September on a year-over-year basis. Analysts cited by Morningstar noted that CPI-W may understate seniors’ actual cost pressures, particularly for healthcare, and pointed to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics ’ CPI-E index for older households, which has historically risen faster than CPI-W. Advocates cite insolvency risk, rising senior hardships The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) said the projected 3.6% COLA for 2028 is likely to arrive against a deteriorating backdrop for older adults, including senior homeowners who may still be making monthly mortgage payments . The group said that seniors are now the country’s fastest-growing homeless population and that many forgo vision, dental and hearing care due to costs. TSCL’s release emphasized that Social Security’s primary trust fund is projected to reach insolvency in 2032, triggering automatic benefit reductions if Congress does not act. The Medicare Part A hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, the group said. That timing elevates the stakes for the next Congress, which will be led by Democrats after their decisive victories in the recent midterm elections . Senators elected in the current cycle will serve from Jan. 3, 2027, through Jan. 3, 2033, overlapping the projected insolvency date. TSCL framed these terms as a key window for any reforms to prevent automatic benefit cuts for millions of retirees. In its agenda for the 120th Congress, TSCL called on lawmakers to: Lift or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap , which exempts wages above $184,500 in 2026 from Social Security taxes. Restore Medicare and Medicaid funding that was reduced under the “One Big Beautiful Bill” passed under the Trump administration in 2025. Add dental, vision and hearing coverage to Medicare. Issue a one-time $1,400 stimulus for seniors to offset what it characterizes as inadequate past COLAs and recent inflation gains. TSCL pointed to Social Security Administration projections, which show that eliminating the taxable wage cap would add “decades” to the trust fund’s life. And the organization’s internal polling indicates broad bipartisan support among seniors for lifting the cap. New bill would tap general revenue, raise debt As advocacy groups push for revenue-raising reforms, a new proposal in the Senate would instead rely on federal borrowing to preserve full benefits. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, has introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. The bill would allow the Department of the Treasury to transfer general fund dollars to Social Security’s retirement trust fund once it becomes insolvent, according to a press release published last week by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB). Under current law, Social Security can only pay benefits from dedicated payroll tax income and trust fund reserves. When the retirement trust fund’s reserves are exhausted — currently projected to be in less than six years — benefits would be cut by about 22% without legislative changes. CRFB estimated that backfilling Social Security with general revenue under Johnson's bill would increase federal debt by $190 trillion over the next 75 years on an inflation-adjusted basis, equal to roughly 165% of gross domestic product. “Paying for Social Security out of the general fund would absolutely explode the national debt, costing a whopping 165% of GDP over 75 years before even considering the economic implications,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said in the release, arguing that the policy could trigger a debt crisis or unsettle bond markets even before it is fully implemented. CRFB characterized the bill as avoiding “the real decisions” needed to repair Social Security’s finances and urged lawmakers to pursue a mix of adjustments — potentially through a bipartisan commission — that would close the program’s funding gap without shifting the shortfall onto the federal balance sheet. Implications for housing and mortgages The trajectory of Social Security and Medicare benefits has direct implications for housing demand and credit risk among the senior segment. Net benefit increases closer to 3% than 3.6% may constrain seniors’ ability to absorb higher housing costs — including the required property tax, insurance and association dues associated with reverse mortgages . items.title: Your real estate listing is stuck and a price drop will not fix it
items.description: There is a category of stuck listing that is going to become more common over the next few years, and most agents have not been trained for it. It is the listing that cannot sell for a reason that has nothing to do with price, photography or effort. It is the listing blocked at the building level, and if we keep coaching agents to treat every slow listing with a price reduction , we are going to watch good professionals burn good listings for no reason. This came up on one of our Power Agent coaching calls. An agent brought me a four-unit situation. The condo had been on the market for 86 days. She had lost two solid buyers. One was all cash, and the all-cash buyer still walked. Any time an all-cash buyer walks, leaders should pay attention, because the one thing you cannot blame is financing. The building had a balcony and structural-compliance issue, the kind of inspection-and-repair requirement that has spread across the country since Surfside and that states like California have written into law for decks and balconies. The repairs had not been started. A new management company had taken over months earlier and was still, in their words, figuring things out. Because the work was un-started, the building landed on the list that does not qualify for conventional Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac financing . The financed buyers were gone instantly. The all-cash buyer pulled the association financials, saw thin reserves and un-started repairs, read it correctly as a poorly run building, and decided the headache was not worth it. Powerfact: Structural-compliance problems do not lower a home's price. They remove a home's buyers. That distinction matters for anyone leading a team, because it changes the coaching . When a building cannot get conventional financing, the buyer pool does not shrink, it collapses to cash buyers willing to tolerate a troubled association. We just watched one of those rare buyers say no. Telling that agent to drop the price would have been coaching malpractice. The price was never the lever. Here's the plan Here is the plan I gave her, and it is the plan I would want every leader teaching. Take it off the market, temporarily. Days on market is a public number, and a climbing one negotiates against your seller before an offer is ever written. Pull the listing before the clock becomes the story. Then, stay hired. This is the step that separates an advisor from an order-taker. Taking a listing off the market should not end the relationship, it should restructure it. The agent and I built a new listing agreement long enough to cover the repair timeline plus fresh marketing afterward at a likely new price. If repairs take a couple of months and the sale takes several more, that is an eight or nine month agreement, not a renewal of the old 90 days. The property comes off the MLS and is not shown, but the agreement stays active. The agent keeps her position. The seller keeps a professional who is still working. Then, advocate for the whole building. I told her to get in front of the management company and the association board, the president and the vice president, and push to expedite repairs that are hurting all 54 owners. This is where a top producer builds a reputation that compounds. When you are the agent pushing a stalled building back into compliance, every owner in that building knows your name, and so does every agent who tried and gave up. In a 54-unit building, that is 54 future listing conversations you just earned by being the one who showed up and did the work nobody else would touch. Rent instead? We also talked through the rent-instead question, because these sellers had already relocated and were carrying the unit. Renting for a year while the building gets sorted is a legitimate option, but it has to be coached with the worst case on the table. In a tenant-friendly jurisdiction an eviction can run six to nine months. Florida's landlord rules are workable. Other markets are not. This property sits in California , and I told her plainly that I do not know California's specifics well enough to promise a timeline, so she needs to find out. Because if the tenant will not leave and removal takes six months, the one-year rental really delivered about six months of clean cash flow. Leaders, this is the kind of worst-case math we owe our sellers, and it is exactly the math an anxious agent skips to avoid an awkward conversation. The larger point for the industry is this. Compliance-driven financing blocks are a growing reality, and they reward the agent who can diagnose, not just discount. The old reflex of lowering price until something moves does not clear a building-level obstacle, and agents who only know that one move will lose listings they could have saved. The professionals who win in this environment are the ones who can look a seller in the eye and say, the problem is not your price, the problem is your building, and here is the plan to fix it. That is the advisor our clients actually need. Serve, don't sell. In a market with this much noise, the agent who clings to a dying listing looks desperate, and the one who calmly takes the sign out of the yard, extends the agreement, and goes to fix the real problem looks like exactly what they are. The one in control. Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com . items.title: Mortgage application payments reveal slight homebuyer affordability gain in October
items.description: Homebuyer affordability improved slightly in October as lower purchase loan amounts offset higher mortgage rates, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)'s Purchase Applications Payment Index (PAPI), released Tuesday. The index, which measures mortgage payments relative to borrower income, decreased 0.3% to a reading of 161.6 in October, down from 162.1 in September. A lower index reading indicates improving affordability . The improvement came despite the national median mortgage payment for purchase applicants rising to $2,236 in October, up $21 (or 0.9%) from $2,215 in September. The median purchase loan application amount fell to $315,424 from $324,022, helping offset a 37-basis-point increase in mortgage rates . “While the median mortgage payment rose $21 in October, payments as a share of earnings edged lower — slightly improving affordability,” Edward Seiler, MBA's associate vice president of housing economics and executive director of the Research Institute for Housing America , said in a statement. Affordability remains weaker than a year ago. The median mortgage payment increased 9.7% from $2,039 in October 2025, while earnings grew 1.6%. As a result, the PAPI was up 8% year over year. “Looking ahead, lower mortgage rates and stronger earnings growth would give prospective buyers more room in their budgets,” Seiler said. The median mortgage payment for Federal Housing Administration ( FHA ) borrowers increased to $1,944 in October, up from $1,906 in September and $1,789 a year earlier. For conventional loan borrowers, the median payment rose to $2,258, up from $2,244 in September and $2,063 in October 2025. Among borrowers applying for lower-payment mortgages, those in the 25th percentile, the median monthly payment increased to $1,536 in October from $1,525 in September. The PAPI for Black households decreased to 162.4 in October from 162.9 in September. For Hispanic households , it fell to 149.6 from 150.1, while the index for white households declined to 162.8 from 163.3. Idaho had the highest PAPI reading in October at 269.8, followed by Nevada at 243.0, Rhode Island at 233.1, Arizona at 215.2 and Utah at 202.7. At the opposite end of the spectrum, Louisiana had the lowest reading at 119.8, followed by Washington, D.C., at 121.5, Alaska at 126.2, Iowa at 127.6 and Connecticut at 131.6. The MBA’s mortgage payment-to- rent ratio also edged higher, increasing to 1.44 at the end of the third quarter from 1.43 at the end of the second quarter. The increase indicates that mortgage payments for home purchases rose slightly relative to rents. The U.S. Census Bureau reported that the national median asking rent increased to $1,541 in the third quarter from $1,531 in the second quarter. The ratio of mortgage payments for lower-payment applicants to median asking rents remained at 0.99 in September. Separately, the MBA’s Builders’ PAPI showed that the median mortgage payment for new-home purchase applicants increased to $2,375 in October, up from $2,307 in September. items.title: Vesteda Sells Close To €1B Rental Houses To Rabobank's BPD To Meet Investor Liquidity
items.description: Dutch residential real estate investor and landlord Vesteda is selling 2,828 existing rental properties to Rabobank for €983M, as Vesteda rebalances its portfolio to meet investor liquidity needs. The Dutch multinational bank will take on the rental assets through an investment in a new residential portfolio to be managed by BPD Fund Management, which it owns, together with the BPD Woningfunds, in which it is an investor. The deal will mean BPD Fund Management oversees a total of 11,000 homes across the Netherlands, with BPD adding 6,000 new rental homes to the country’s housing stock annually. Courtesy of Vesteda A residential asset in Eindhoven, part of a portfolio sold by Vesteda to BPD As the Netherlands faces a steep housing shortage, the trio of Vesteda, BPD and Rabobank have pledged to invest in affordable and sustainable housing. The rental properties sold are spread across the Netherlands, with 43% being single-family homes and 57% apartments. The average monthly rent of the properties is €1,200, with most having an energy rating of A or B. “BPD Woningfonds is adding new mid-rental segment homes to the housing market," BPD CEO Harm Janssen said in a statement. “The new residential portfolio will ensure that existing affordable rental homes remain available to middle-income households.” Following the transaction, all rents and tenancy conditions under the current agreement are set to remain in place, with more than 2,800 of the rental properties sold staying within the rental pool. While the transaction is still subject to approval by the Dutch Consumers and Markets Authority, the transfer is expected to be completed in early 2027. Vesteda manages a rental portfolio of approximately 28,000 rental homes with a total value of €10.8B and located in key economic hubs and metropolitan areas in the Netherlands. The largest institutional investor in residential real estate in the country said the deal will aid the ongoing “stability of the residential fund,” according to a press statement. Courtesy of Vesteda Watertorenweg, a residential asset in Rotterdam, the Netherlands sold by Vesteda to BPD News of the transaction comes months after Vesteda’s shareholders limited the amount of redemption requests that investors in its main residential funds could make to €756M, following redemption requests in the Vesteda Residential Fund that soared to €4.1B, the equivalent of 52% of its assets, this March. Following an extraordinary general meeting on June 26, Vesteda agreed that investors in its fund can sell their stakes annually, rather than only once every seven years. To cover the inevitable gaps, Vesteda aims to free up capital worth 7.5% of the fund’s equity each year, although this amount is not guaranteed. Speaking at Bisnow ’s Netherlands State of the Market event last week at KIT in Amsterdam , Vesteda CEO Astrid Schlüter said that while the Dutch residential market has seen many transactions this year, the rental market continues to shrink on balance. Close to 13,000 rental homes were sold to parties with privatization strategies, and fewer than 11,000 new rental units were added during the first three quarters of 2026, Schlüter said. “The ambition to add 100,000 new homes to the Dutch housing market is still far away, and the underlying demand isn’t gone,” she said. Schlüter added that rising interest rates and geopolitical and economic uncertainties are affecting the residential market. Still, she noted that the residential sector, like all others, follows its own cycles. “Investing in Dutch residential is for the long term,” she said. items.title: McDonald's Franchisees Push Back Against Pricey Renovation Plans
items.description: As the fast-food sector struggles nationwide, the franchisees powering its most ubiquitous brand are pushing back against requests to shell out for expensive renovations. Wikimedia Commons/Dirk Tussing McDonald’s is asking the franchisees who operate 95% of its stores to spend $800K to upgrade each restaurant as sales falter, Bloomberg reported . Many of these operators see that as a tough pill to swallow after they each spent at least $35K on tech upgrades, including the chain’s new artificial intelligence -powered drive-thru ordering system. The new program rolled out by the burger chain’s central office, branded as “Next,” would include sesame seed ceiling designs and french fry-shaped outdoor shades that have reportedly tested well with customers. It also calls for tearing down walls between the dining room and the kitchen so customers can see workers preparing their food. Many of those barriers were installed at the central office’s behest less than a decade ago, sometimes at a price exceeding $100K. U.S. franchisees are obligated to spend $400K on remodels every decade or so, but the Next plan goes beyond that, so McDonald’s is expected to foot some of the bill. Some franchisees have told McDonald's they won't launch the renovations unless it shows them evidence that each aspect will yield financial benefits, Bloomberg reported. Cost-conscious consumers have become increasingly wary of the chain , which is no longer broadly seen as a reliable spot for an affordable meal. That has contributed to a nearly 10% decline in its stock price over the past year, even as it has worked to roll out more value options. The pushback from operators comes as fast-food franchisees have been filing for bankruptcy at a growing clip around the country. Last week, that list expanded to include the 84-location KFC operator Tasty Chick’n, whose sales began to decline in 2023. The 15-location Pennsylvania-based Papa John’s franchisee Papa ZHS also submitted a Chapter 11 filing earlier this month. McDonald’s most direct rival is also plotting renovations. Burger King has launched a website to field customer feedback about specific stores as the company continues its “Reclaim the Flame” turnaround strategy launched in 2022. It includes a goal of modernizing up to 90% of the company’s locations by 2028. Burger King’s sales grew 8.4% last quarter, while McDonald’s reported that sales fell by 0.2%. items.title: L&G Enters Development Lending With Fairbanks Studios Finance Deal
items.description: Courtesy of Oxygen Studios L&G's first financing is supporting the construction of a film and television studio campus in Hertfordshire. L&G is expanding its UK real estate debt business into development lending, with its first financing supporting the construction of a film and television studio campus in Hertfordshire. The lender provided a development and stabilisation loan for an undisclosed amount to BNP Paribas Asset Management Alts to finance Fairbanks Studios, a purpose-built film and television production campus in Elstree. The facility comes from L&G’s £33B private credit platform within its asset management business, deploying capital on behalf of external clients and its institutional retirement business. The move marks an expansion of L&G’s real estate debt strategy, with its new development lending platform targeting loans of £10M to more than £100M. It will finance ground-up development, refurbishment and completed schemes that have yet to stabilise. Target sectors include residential, student accommodation, prime offices, selective retail and alternative real estate. Fairbanks Studios will consist of approximately 266K SF of studio space, including five soundstages, workshops, production support facilities and offices. The site is in Elstree, one of the UK’s established film and television production locations, and the development is targeting BREEAM Outstanding and energy performance certificate A ratings, with all-electric studio operations and a rooftop solar photovoltaic system. BNP Paribas AM Alts acquired the site on behalf of clients in 2024 and subsequently secured planning permission for its redevelopment. Construction is now progressing. “Expanding into development lending is a natural extension of our established UK real estate debt business, enabling us to provide institutional capital to high-quality real estate projects across the UK,” L&G Head of Real Estate Debt, UK & Europe James Spencer-Jones said in a statement. “Fairbanks Studios exemplifies the type of opportunity we're looking to support. It combines an excellent location, high-quality sponsorship and delivery of product in a supply-constrained market,” he added. Film and high-end television production spending reached £6.8B last year, up 22% on 2024, according to the British Film Institute, with £4B attributable to high-end television and £2.8B to feature films, underlining the UK's continued appeal to international production companies, particularly U.S.-backed studios and streaming platforms. However, the development pipeline is substantial, with the Valuation Office Agency previously identifying a potential increase in English and Welsh studio stage space from 4.5M SF in 2023 to 6M SF by April 2026. As a result, developers are increasingly focused on the quality, location and supporting infrastructure of facilities, seeking proximity to established production clusters, specialist suppliers and skilled labour. recent_coverage.title: Machine Investment Group Buys 490-Unit Apartment Community in North Dallas
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Machine Investment Group 与 RPM Living 收购北达拉斯 490 套 75 West，项目含 10,800 平方英尺零售空间；交易通过贷款方主导的场外流程完成，RPM Living 将负责管理。

recent_coverage.title: Another Small Victory For Mortgage Rates
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Mortgage News Daily 称，11 月 19 日 30 年期固定按揭利率为 7.45%，下降 0.01%；债券收益率随股市走弱回落，帮助利率小幅下行。

recent_coverage.title: Anthropic's Record IPO Reverberates Across Data Center Sector
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Anthropic IPO 募资 813 亿美元，部分资金将用于计算能力和数据中心；报道同时指出，AI 基建投资回报、估值及社区反对仍带来不确定性。

recent_coverage.title: U.S. Retail Monthly Foot Traffic & Sales Analysis | October 2026
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Colliers 报告称，10 月美国零售销售同比增长 6.9%，客流增长 1.6%；核心零售销售增长 5.5%，家居相关支出仍面临住房市场挑战。

recent_coverage.title: Progress Residential, owner Pretium Partners settle FTC rental fee suit for $50M
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Progress Residential 及其所有者 Pretium Partners 与 FTC 就租赁费用诉讼达成 5,000 万美元和解；报道称这是该机构针对房东金额最大的一次执法行动。

recent_coverage.title: Houston new-home sales dip to lowest level of 2026
recent_coverage.summary_zh: HomesUSA.com 数据显示，休斯敦 10 月售出 1,724 套新屋，同比下降 12.7%；新屋签约量为 1,447 套，同比下降 17.8%，均为年内低位。

recent_coverage.title: Office Development Hits 10-Year Low as Demand for Top Space Climbs
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Cushman & Wakefield 称，美国办公楼在建面积为 2,300 万平方英尺，较 2020 年高点下降 83%；其研究人员表示，优质办公楼空置率下降并支撑租金增长。

recent_coverage.title: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012
recent_coverage.summary_zh: ATTOM 报告称，2026 年第三季度住宅购房贷款为 729,968 笔，环比下降 9%，为 2012 年以来第三季度最低；机构将负担能力承压与按揭利率上升联系起来。

recent_coverage.title: Brookfield Bets $110M On Resorts Company Rolling Up Independent Campgrounds
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Brookfield 计划以 1.1 亿美元收购 Open Road Resorts 少数股权，资金将用于收购更多露营地；这笔投资针对户外住宿细分市场，不足以代表更广泛地产资本趋势。

recent_coverage.title: MarketBeat New York City Capital Markets Q3 2026
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Cushman & Wakefield 数据显示，纽约市第三季度投资销售额为 56 亿美元，环比下降 30.7%；年初至今销售额为 220 亿美元，与去年同期基本持平。

recent_coverage.title: Mortgage Rates
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Freddie Mac 报告称，截至 11 月 19 日，30 年期固定按揭利率平均为 7.28%，高于上周的 7.11% 和一年前的 6.26%；15 年期利率为 6.66%。

recent_coverage.title: Monthly Housing Payments Fell to Lowest Level in Nearly 2 Months–But Rates Are Climbing Again
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Redfin 的截至 11 月 15 日四周数据显示，成屋签约量周环比下降 0.3%，为 2021 年有记录以来最低；房价同比下降 0.4%，但按揭利率回升可能加重购房压力。

recent_coverage.title: Large Median Price Gap Keeps New Homes More Affordable Than Existing Homes
recent_coverage.summary_zh: NAHB 指出，2026 年第三季度新屋价格中位数为 393,300 美元，低于成屋的 432,900 美元；但典型家庭购买新屋和成屋分别需用收入的 33% 和 36% 支付按揭。

recent_coverage.title: Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028
recent_coverage.summary_zh: 5 个住房及按揭行业团体请求 FHFA 将公寓协会最低储备金要求从 2027 年 1 月 4 日推迟至 2028 年 1 月 4 日，并称新规可能扰动公寓融资和住房供应。

recent_coverage.title: Colliers Brokers Sale of 365-Unit Apartment Community in Katy, Texas
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Colliers 促成德州 Katy 的 The Vic at Jordan Ranch 公寓社区出售，该项目有 365 套住宅；买方为未披露的机构投资公司，交易价格未披露。

recent_coverage.title: Parkland Communities secures $50M development financing, begins Highland Brook in Dacula
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Parkland Communities 获得 5,000 万美元循环生产融资，首笔 1,500 万美元用于佐治亚州 Highland Brook 项目；资金可用于土地、开发成本及新屋建设。

recent_coverage.title: Multifamily Permitting’s Share Rebounds as Single-Family Declines
recent_coverage.summary_zh: RealPage 称，2026 年 10 月多户住宅许可年化为 475,000 套，环比下降 5.2%、同比基本持平；其占住宅许可比例升至 36.7%，部分源于独栋住宅许可走弱。

recent_coverage.title: Office REIT Sells Reston Property To Local Firm For 30% Of 2014 Price
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Office Properties Income Trust 将一处空置率略高于一半的弗吉尼亚办公楼以 1,210 万美元售出，远低于 2014 年的 4,100 万美元；该 REIT 于 2025 年申请破产保护。

recent_coverage.title: Thorofare Capital Provides $16.7M Bridge Loan for Metro Dallas Medical Office Building
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Thorofare Capital 为德州 Mesquite 一栋 64,890 平方英尺的医疗办公楼提供 1,670 万美元过桥贷款；借款方未披露，单笔融资不足以说明整体 CRE 信贷状况。

recent_coverage.title: Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows
recent_coverage.summary_zh: HousingWire 专栏作者认为，需求不足使住宅建设许可接近疫情时期低位；Census 显示，10 月许可年化为 1,295,000 套，较前一月修订值 1,398,000 下降 7.4%。

recent_coverage.title: Bank Branch Costs Hinge More on Market Than Management, JLL Finds
recent_coverage.summary_zh: JLL 报告称，美国银行 2026 年上半年新开网点数量超过关闭数量；其研究指出，12 个市场中每平方英尺设施运营成本最高与最低相差 2.6 倍。

recent_coverage.title: Mortgage Rates Move Slightly Lower
recent_coverage.summary_zh: 平均高等级 30 年固定利率为 7.46%，连续第 2 天回落；但较上周初高近 0.20%，报道认为 11 月下半月利率可能受假日交易影响而波动。

recent_coverage.title: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Realtor.com 称 10 月中位挂牌租金为 $1,692，较上年同期上升 $1（+0.1%），为 2023 年 6 月以来首次同比上涨；2026Q3 完工量和新开工分别为 330,000 和 403,000，同比下降 26% 和 9.2%。

recent_coverage.title: BTR Operators Push For Treasury To Loosen Rules As Consolidation Looms
recent_coverage.summary_zh: 拟议财政部规则要求持有至少 350 套单户出租房的机构投资者先制定书面 BTR 计划，并限制证书签发 18 个月后购入房屋；运营商称或压制资本流入和新建社区。

recent_coverage.title: Fitch warns of growing balance-sheet strain at top nonbank mortgage firms
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Fitch 将 Pennymac、Planet 和 Freedom Mortgage 的长期发行人评级展望由稳定调为负面，称高杠杆和 MSR 暴露拖累信用状况，2027 年盈利或受利率环境约束。

recent_coverage.title: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report
recent_coverage.summary_zh: NAR 报告显示，10 月住宅签约量环比下降 4.7%、同比下降 16.7%，四大区域均下滑；首席经济学家称连续两个月创纪录低位或预示第四季度成屋销售收官疲弱。

recent_coverage.title: Sherwood Equities Sells Hudson Yards Development Site For $100M: The N.Y. Deal Sheet
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Sherwood Equities 将 460 10th Ave. 的 17K SF 住宅开发地块以 $100M 售予 Joyland Group；买方与 Prospect Development 计划建设 34 层、456 套公寓，卖方出售原因不明。

recent_coverage.title: New Residential Construction Press Release
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Census 显示，10 月新屋开工年化季调后为 1,309,000，较 9 月修订值上升 9.9%、同比上升 2.8%；营建许可为 1,295,000，较 9 月修订值下降 7.4%、同比下降 8.7%。

recent_coverage.title: New Home Lot Supply Index
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Zonda 的 New Home Lot Supply Index 在 2026Q3 升至 88.5，同比上升 20.8%、较 2Q26 上升 3.9%，市场评级转为“供应适当”；研究机构提醒，可负担性压力、激励措施及土地成本挑战仍在。

recent_coverage.title: HUD finalizes rule targeting mixed-immigration-status households receiving aid
recent_coverage.summary_zh: HUD 于 11 月 12 日最终确定新规，要求住房援助家庭所有成员证明美国公民身份或合资格移民身份；规则 12 月 14 日生效，NLIHC 估计或影响多达 80,000 人，相关诉讼已提起。

recent_coverage.title: Fed Officials Expect Further Interest Rate Hikes After Pausing Last Month
recent_coverage.summary_zh: 10 月 FOMC 以 10 比 2 维持隔夜利率 3.75%--4%；纪要称部分官员认为未来加息可能适宜，少数人考虑 12 月更大幅度加息，CME FedWatch 显示半个百分点加息概率为 5%。

recent_coverage.title: Morgan Completes 345-Unit Multifamily Project in North Austin
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Morgan 完成北奥斯汀 The Watson 多户项目，共 345 套，建筑为 7 层，含单间及一至三居室；工作室租金起价约 $1,600／月，项目配有泳池、健身中心和共享办公空间。

recent_coverage.title: IPA Negotiates Sale of 399-Unit Apartment Community in Grapevine, Texas
recent_coverage.summary_zh: IPA 代表 Greystar 出售德州 Grapevine 的 The Preserve 公寓社区；项目建于 2020 年，共 399 套，平均面积 968 SF，买方未披露。

recent_coverage.title: HOUSTON RENTERS KEEP THE MARKET MOVING IN OCTOBER
recent_coverage.summary_zh: HAR 称 10 月休斯敦地区单户住宅出租 3,850 套，同比增 3.5%，平均租金升至 $2,293；联排与公寓出租量增 9.1%，但库存继续扩张，新挂牌增 1.7%、在售增 3.3%。

recent_coverage.title: MarketBeat SF Bay Area Life Sciences Q3 2026
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Cushman & Wakefield 称，湾区生命科学就业在 2026Q3 为 104,400 个岗位，空置率为 28.5%，季度租赁活动达 828,511 SF；但平均 NNN 要价降至每月每 SF $5.53。

recent_coverage.title: Congress Puts Up $216M For Energy Department Relocation From Forrestal
recent_coverage.summary_zh: 参议院委员会批准 $215.6M，用于能源部员工迁出 1.8M SF 的 Forrestal 办公楼群及新总部准备；GSA 可考虑该楼的其他用途或处置，但尚无时间表。

recent_coverage.title: Griffin Capital Starts Work on 132 Lakeside Village Rental Townhomes
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Griffin Capital 在 Flower Mound 推进 Lakeside Village 的 132 套租赁联排住宅，建设成本预计 $40M，计划于 2028 年 8 月完工；项目占地近 10 英亩，分布于 26 栋建筑。

recent_coverage.title: Kisco Senior Living Lands $52M Refi on San Rafael Senior Living Community
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Kisco Senior Living 为 San Rafael 的 123 套老年社区获得 $52.2M Freddie Mac 再融资，期限 10 年、全期只付息并含现金提取；物业过去 24 个月入住率保持在 91% 以上。

recent_coverage.title: Partners Capital Acquires Terraces at Windward Retail Center in Metro Atlanta
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Partners Capital 收购亚特兰大都会区 84,620 SF 的 Terraces at Windward，物业售出时有 14 个租户；该基金计划首年投入超过 $1M，改造外立面及停车场。

recent_coverage.title: October 2026 multifamily starts and permits signal a potential shift in supply outlook
recent_coverage.summary_zh: Zillow 称 10 月全国多户新屋开工升至 433,000 套，较 9 月上升 25.5%；多户许可降至 475,000，较 9 月下降 5.2%，但全国租客需求同比增 22.1%，买方需求仍弱。

recent_coverage.title: Homeownership Remains a Key to Household Wealth
recent_coverage.summary_zh: NAHB 引述美联储 SCF 称，2025 年美国自住住宅合计价值 $47.2 trillion，占家庭总资产 26%；66% 家庭拥有自住住宅，报告强调住房对财富积累与家庭财务安全的重要性。
